content: Even in very constructive cases, where the resulting terms don't have any axioms, there seem to be axioms like Classical.choice added to every theorem that uses grind. How is that possible when the term does not use it? And is there a way to disable this?
grind always uses choice since it proves by contradiction, and I believe there's no way to disable it
Do you have an example (that can be proven without choice) where simp does this? You can probably make it stop using simp only

For simp:

theorem test : 3 = 1 + 2 :=
  by simp
#print axioms test -- 'test' depends on axioms: [propext]

Well this uses the docs#Nat.reduceAdd simproc which uses docs#eq_self (for some reason) which depends on propext.
But you can just rfl here
Well yes of course you can use rfl, the point was that it adds axioms for even extremely trivial statements that could be proved by rfl
But I could see why that's reasonable and propext is extremely innnocuous

If you don't like that simproc you can use simp [-Nat.reduceAdd]. In this case you'll find that simp will then use Nat.right_eq_add, and unfortunately that depends on all 3 axioms, but that's a different problem
Nat.reduceAdd doesn't use eq_self, simp itself does, it's one of the simp lemmas that's even available on simp only.
It's what simp uses to close goals of the form a = a (by rewriting them to True)
Is there a list of all simp lemmas that are available in the bare simp only? Do any of them depend on choice?
btw Jason Carr you might be interested in #general > Make mathlib less dependent on choice
Yeah here. Well but it's just docs#eq_self and docs#iff_self, which are used to close a = a and a ↔ a goals, respectively. Both require docs#propext but nothing else.

You can even disable them if you really want to:

example : 1 = 1 := by
  simp only [-eq_self, -iff_self] -- fails

In general I think we just use these axioms because they are convenient. For example, without propext, you'd need to do all sort of weird congruence argumentation (which I did in https://github.com/Rob23oba/lean4-no-axioms/ as an experiment)

Some forces seem too strong:

theorem test : 3 = 1 + 2 := by
  simp [-eq_self, -of_eq_true, -eq_true_of_decide, -Eq.refl]

/--
info: theorem test : 3 = 1 + 2 :=
of_eq_true (eq_true_of_decide (Eq.refl true))
-/
#guard_msgs in
#print test

/-- info: 'test' depends on axioms: [propext] -/
#guard_msgs in
#print axioms test
Well, it fails with simp [-Nat.reduceEqDiff, -eq_self]

Sometimes I've thought it would be an interesting metaprogramming project to create a proof rewriter that attempts to eliminate choice. The idea would be that it would take the elaborated proof term then go through an expression, transforming p (Classical.choice h) into h.elim fun x => p x, and resynthesizing Decidable instances. I'm guessing that rewriting proofs post hoc will handle most cases where a tactic like grind might have been able to be designed to avoid choice. Plus, the tactic doesn't need to be modified for this application, which would be a significant undertaking, and proof rewriting might even be a more effective strategy in the end, since a purely constructive version of grind might be too complicated or be too conservative.

Maybe the project is doomed to fail though, since it's not clear how you can systematically eliminate arbitrary case splits (uses of LEM) — though I'd hope that Decidable resynthesis might be enough for common cases.

I see, that simproc adds eq_true_of_decide and Eq.refl!
But who adds of_eq_true?

I'd expect that to be docs#Lean.Meta.simpTargetCore itself. When simp reduces a goal to True, then that means it's built a proof h : originalGoal = True, so it uses of_eq_true to close the original goal.
Ah so docs#Lean.Elab.Tactic.simpOnlyBuiltins isn't exhaustive

I don't see the issue?
what do you mean issue?

Surely if you're claiming that it's not impossible then instead of asking why it's impossible you should just show that it's possible? And if you fail then you'll have answered your own question.
surely the person who claimed that it is impossible first should explain why?

The proof of docs#Quotient.exact lifts the quotient relation to a relation Quotient s → Quotient s → Prop which requires getting an equality from the equivalence a₁ ≈ b₁ ↔ a₂ ≈ b₂. I don't know whether it's completely unavoidable to do it otherwise but I don't know of another way that doesn't use docs#propext.

The proof of docs#Quotient.exact lifts the quotient relation to a relation Quotient s → Quotient s → Prop which requires getting an equality from the equivalence a₁ ≈ b₁ ↔ a₂ ≈ b₂. I don't know whether it's completely unavoidable to do it otherwise but I don't know of another way that doesn't use docs#propext.

I think that just requires Quot.sound, no? I don't see why there's any need for propext

A type of theorem that needs propext to state would be quite ugly since it would have to rely on rewriting over these equalities. But it could just as well use heterogeneous equality to hide that fact
No it does require propext for that proof path. We have f a b := a ≈ b and the quotient lift requires a₁ ≈ a₂ → b₁ ≈ b₂ → f a₁ b₁ = f a₂ b₂, i.e. a₁ ≈ a₂ → b₁ ≈ b₂ → (a₁ ≈ b₁) = (a₂ ≈ b₂).

I don't see the relevance, and neither I nor lean find any axiom use in Quot.exact,
The eliminator for quotients does not require any axioms because these are consistent with the definition Quot α := α. Only the actual quotienting, r a b -> Quot.mk a = Quot.mk b requires anything

but in any case I don't think propext is worth focusing much attention on compared to choice. I am aware of no interesting models where propext fails, given that it holds in every topos as well as in univalent settings (of course lean does not support the latter at all in this version)

I think this may be solvable. Or rather one can simply check the uses of the contradiction. If negations don't escape into values then we can eliminate the double negation.
E.g. if we prove (¬P → ⊥), but we only do so by applying that argument, and the values it applies to also don't capture any negations, we can lift. Effectively, attempt local CPS by transforming into (forall R, (P → R) → R). In that case, we can eliminate.

For EM likewise:

theorem EM_poly :
  ∀ {P Q: Prop},
  (∀ (R: Prop), P ∨ (P → R) → (Q → R) → R) →
  Q :=
  by
    intros P Q HQ
    let r := (HQ (P ∨ Q) (Or.inr Or.inl) Or.inr)
    cases r with
    | inl p => exact (HQ Q (Or.inl p) id)
    | inr q => exact q
